In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as "drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The SNaPshot Version 4 clinical test detects common 
mutations in 23 cancer genes. The SNaPshot multiplex assay tests for somatic 
variants at 90 different loci. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples.

cancer genes. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is followed by mutation 
detection using single base extension sequencing technology (SNaPshot, Applied 
Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using primers flanking EGFR 
exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect in-frame activating 
insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be detected using 
SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA analyzer. The 
average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay has been

NEGATIVE: No mutations were identified in this sample, including within the EGFR

Approximately 50% of lung adenocarcinomas will possess a mutation within at

TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as "drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The SNaPshot Version 4 clinical test detects common 
mutations in 23 cancer genes. The SNaPshot multiplex assay tests for somatic 
variants at 90 different loci. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele. 
 
This test was developed, and its performance characteristics were determined by 
the MGH Diagnostic Molecular Pathology Laboratory. It has not been approved by 
the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. The FDA has determined that such 
clearance is not necessary. This test is used for clinical purposes. Pursuant to 
the requirements of CLIA 88, this laboratory has established and verified the 
test accuracy and precision.

INDICATION FOR TEST - Lung adenocarcinoma 
 
FISH RESULTS: 
 
Fluorescence in situ hybridization of paraffin tumor tissue using a 
break-apart probe to the ALK gene revealed no rearrangement of the ALK locus. 
 
ISCN  REMOVED_CASE_ID  nomenclature: nuc ish (ALK x 2)[48/50] 
 
 
INTERPRETATION: 
 
NORMAL 
These results indicate NO ALK rearrangement in this case (block  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID ). 
 
TEST INFORMATION: 
Rearrangement involving the ALK gene on 2p23 with the  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  gene on 2p21 is 
present in approximately 5% of lung adenocarcinomas. Lung tumors with ALK 
rearrangement have been shown to respond to ALK kinase inhibitors (1). In 
addition, in 70-80% of ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphomas (ALCL), ALK 
is paired with Nucleophosmin (NPM) on 5q35, and with a variety of other genes in 
the remaining. ALK rearrangements have also been described in other tumors 
including inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors, neural tumors, and in some 
subtypes of breast cancer and of rhabdomyosarcomas. Almost invariably, ALK 
translocations result in chimeric proteins containing a 5'-end partner fused to 
the ALK tyrosine kinase domain at the 3'-end. Deregulated ALK activity has an 
oncogenic effect, and targeted therapies against this kinase are currently being 
analyzed to treat cancers harboring rearrangements in the ALK locus. 
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using formalin-fixed 
paraffin-embedded specimens has been shown to be an effective method for 
determining presence of these translocations. Briefly, 5-micron sections of 
formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor material were prepared and an H&E 
section reviewed to select regions for hybridization that contain a majority of 
tumor cells. An ALK break-apart probe (REPEAT-FREE (RF) POSEIDON FISH Probe on 
ALK (2p23) Break, Kreatech Diagnostics, Amsterdam, Netherlands) was hybridized, 
and used to calculate the number of cells out of 50 scored containing a 
rearrangement. An ALK rearrangement is reported if more than 15% of cells show 
split signals. CPT codes for this test:  REMOVED_CASE_ID  (morphometric analysis, in situ 
hybridization, each probe, manual) x 2.

keratin positive ( REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID / REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID , Pan-K, Cam REMOVED_DATE and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID /6). The spindle cells range 
from rounded to a more spindled appearance, have high grade nuclei, and these

p63 and calponin consistent with myoepithelial differentiation. The tumor has a 
lobulated border which is irregular and infiltrative. 
The staining pattern excludes an unusual phyllodes tumor. A malignant 
adenomyoepithelioma is favored given the distinctive morphological appearance 
and supporting immunostains. Although criteria which predict local recurrence 
and the development of distant metastases are not definitively established, 
available reports in the literature suggest that the presence of myoepithelial 
and epithelial nuclear pleomorphism and atypia, along with mitoses > REMOVED_DATE HPF, 
necrosis, and a lobulated or infiltrative border favors a diagnosis of 
"malignant adenomyoepithelioma". The two largest series have been published by 
Drs. Tavassoli and Page (see references below). Dr. S. Lester, & Dr. A. 
Richardson have also reviewed this case and agree with the diagnosis.

TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as "drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The assay SNaPshot Version 3 detects mutations in 68 
different loci from 14 cancer genes. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

Granulomatous inflammation with patchy necrosis and fibrinous pneumonia. 
Focus of fungal pseudohyphae consistent with candida species. 
There is no evidence of malignancy.

There is no evidence of malignancy. 
 
 
Note: The lung shows a diffuse infiltrate of lymphocytes and histiocytes with 
poorly formed granulomas with giant cells. There is evidence of small vessel 
angiitis and patchy parenchymal necrosis with fibrinous pneumonia. The 
differential diagnosis includes infection and Wegener's granulomatosis. The 
focal fungal infection is judged to represent a focus of superinfection and does 
not likely account for the underlying pathology. No sulfur granules are 
present. Wegener's and causes of autoimmune angiitis should be excluded 
serologically. GMS, gram, AFB, Fite, and elastic stains were examined. Ig REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  
immunostain is negative. In situ hybridization for EBV to exclude lymphomatoid 
granulomatosis will be separately reported in an addendum.

SQUAMOUS METAPLASIA OF LACTIFEROUS DUCTS with associated subareolar chronic 
granulomatous inflammation, see NOTE 
Uninvolved breast parenchyma with apocrine cysts. 
Skin with scar and prior procedure site changes. 
NOTE: Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (SMOLD) is also known as 
recurrent subareolar abscess and periductal mastitis. This unusual disease is 
mostly seen in smokers where it presents as a painful erythematous subareolar 
mass which fails to heal following incision and drainage of the "abscess". The 
pathology is keratinizing squamous metaplasia deep in the nipple ducts which 
causes them to dilate and then rupture producing a non-infectious chronic 
granulomatous inflammatory response (the "abscess") which often drains to the 
overlying skin as a purulent exudate via the offending nipple duct or a sinus 
tract.

anterior to posterior. The specimen is covered by a skin ellipse, measuring 
13.5cm x 7.0cm with 3.0cm areola, centered by a 1.4cm everted nipple (0.7 
cm anterior to posterior). There is a 2.5cm well-healed scar in the lateral 
side of the areola. The nipple orifice oozes white thick purulent material. No 
additional fistula tracts are seen either on the areolar or on adjacent skin. 
The deep margin is an intact fascia and is inked black. Sectioning reveals a 
fibrous breast parenchyma (75% fibrous admixed with adipose tissue). In the

nipple and 2.5cm from the deep margin. The entire nipple/areolar area to

substantial pan-dermal infiltrate by neutrophils with associated superficial 
ulceration in the absence of primary endothelial occlusive alterations and 
zonal necrosis would favor pyoderma gangrenosum. The extent of subcutaneous 
involvement is, however, somewhat unusual for this entity, although secondary 
involvement from the overlying dermis and nature of sampling [debridement of 
more advanced regions] may in part account for this finding). It is 
recommended that the final diagnostic assessment also include consideration of 
correlative clinical parameters, notably exclusion of an infectious cause. In 
addition, if at anytime the clinical parameters continue to raise the 
possibility of necrotizing fasciitis (as opposed to an atypically deep/advanced 
manifestation of pyoderma gangrenosum), sampling of an early evolving lesion or 
lesion edge (as opposed to a debridement sampling) is suggested.

Lymph node with changes most consistent with reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, (see 
note). 
 
Note: The specimen consists of two cores of lymphoid tissue consistent with 
lymph node and cores of fibroadipose tissue. The lymphoid tissue shows reactive 
lymphoid follicles and an interfollicular area with a polymorphous mixture of 
lymphocytes, histiocytes, few immunoblasts, and plasma cells. Clear cells 
consistent with monocytoid B cells are present, adjacent to some follicles. A 
few large lymphoid cells with prominent nucleoli are present among the 
monocytoid B cells. 
 
Flow cytometry (see below) shows no abnormal B or T-cell population. 
Immunostains show staining of follicles and monocytoid B cells with  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID . There 
are many interfollicular T cells ( REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID +).  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  highlights scattered medium-sized

cytomegalovirus is negative. No atypical cells are detected with cytokeratin 
cocktail ( REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID , 3; Cam5.2). In-situ hybridization for kappa and lambda 
immunoglobulin light chains highlights scattered polytypic plasma cells. 
 
Overall, the findings are most consistent with reactive lymphoid hyperplasia; 
however, they are somewhat atypical, and if clinically indicated, excision of 
the lymph node could be considered.

TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as"drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The SNaPshot Version 4 clinical test detects common 
mutations in 23 cancer genes. The SNaPshot multiplex assay tests for somatic 
variants at 90 different loci. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as "drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The assay SNaPshot Version 3 detects mutations in 68 
different loci from 14 cancer genes. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

amplification status. Briefly, 5-micron sections of formalin-fixed

TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as "drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The assay SNaPshot Version 3 detects mutations in 68 
different loci from 14 cancer genes. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

INTERPRETATION: 
NEOPLASTIC CELLS PRESENT. 
 
DIAGNOSIS: 
- Low-grade spindle cell neoplasm (see NOTE). 
 
 
B. BREAST CELLBLOCK, LEFT, 5:00: 
- Rare plump spindle cells, consistent with a low-grade spindle cell neoplasm 
(see NOTE). 
- Multiple levels examined. 
 
 
NOTE: Cytology shows a cellular population of plump spindle cells with low-grade 
atypia predominantly arranged as single cells with loosely cohesive clusters 
clinging to branching capillary vessels. Scattered throughout there are cells 
with ganglion-like morphology, binucleated forms and rare multinucleated cells. 
Scattered cells also contain apoptotic debris/cell fragments. There are no 
mitoses and no necrosis. Some cells are attached to a thin fibrous stroma, but 
myxoid change is not identified. An epithelial component is not identified. 
 
Immunohistochemistry Tumor cells are positive for SMA. They are negative for 
 REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID : REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID /Cam5.2, p63 and desmin.  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  is noncontributory due to exhaustion of 
neoplastic cells on block. 
 
Overall, the cytomorphologic is consistent with a low-grade spindle cell 
neoplasm. The differential diagnosis is broad but limited immunohistochemical 
profile suggests myofibroblastic differentiation (such as nodular fasciitis, 
mammary-type myofibroblastoma/ cellular PASH, or the stromal component of a 
fibroepithelial neoplasm, such as phyllodes tumor). However, due to the limited 
staining panel that could be performed, a more specific interpretation cannot be 
made and a low-grade malignancy cannot be ruled out. Complete excision for 
histologic examination is recommended.

HYPERCELLULAR MARROW WITH INVOLVEMENT BY A LOW GRADE B-CELL LYMPHOMA / 
LEUKEMIA. 
(SEE NOTE.) 
 
NOTE: The bone marrow biopsy specimen is adequate for evaluation. The bone 
marrow clot specimen contains very scant marrow particles. The marrow 
cellularity is overall approximately 80%. The myeloid-to-erythroid ratio is 
normal. Myeloid maturation is complete. Erythroid maturation is complete. 
Megakaryocytes appear adequate. Multiple large lymphoid aggregates are present, 
in both a paratrabecular and non-trabecular distribution. The lymphoid cells 
are small to medium-sized with irregular nuclear contours and variably abundant 
pale cytoplasm. The lymphoid cells overall comprise approximately 50-60% of 
total marrow cellularity, and occupy 40-50% of the marrow space. Granulomas 
are not identified. Both H&E and Giemsa stains were examined to evaluate the 
biopsy. Reticulin stain shows 1-2+/4 fiber staining. 
 
The aspirate smear is adequate for evaluation. A 300-cell differential count 
reveals: 34% myeloid precursors, 30% erythroid precursors, 27% lymphocytes, 2% 
monocytes, 4% eosinophils, 1% basophils, 1% promyelocytes, 0% blasts, and 1% 
plasma cells. Myeloid maturation is normal. Erythroid maturation is normal 
except for late mitoses. Megakaryocytes appear normal. 
The lymphocytes are predominantly small forms with condensed chromatin, scant 
basophilic cytoplasm, and mild nuclear irregularity. The proportion of 
lymphocytes is highly variable from one area to another, with some fields being 
predominantly composed of lymphocytes. A smear stained for iron shows abundant 
iron stores; no ringed sideroblasts are identified. 
 
CBC results from REMOVED_DATE are as follows: WBC: REMOVED_DATE  HCT: REMOVED_DATE  PLT: 73. 
Auto differential from REMOVED_DATE  35% polys, 61% lymphocytes, 3% monocytes, 1% 
eosinophils, and 0% basophils. 
Review of the peripheral smear reveals mature leukocytes with scattered mature 
lymphoid cells with delicate cytoplasmic processes, consistent with villous 
lymphocytes. 
 
SUMMARY: In a patient with massive splenomegaly, the findings are suspicious 
for marrow involvement by splenic marginal zone lymphoma. Immunostains are in 
progress to evaluate the specimen further; results will be reported in an 
addendum. 
See also results of flow cytometry (ML-10- REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID ), which shows a clonal B cell 
population. Also see results of cytogenetics (CG-10- REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID ).

Immunohistochemistry reveals that the lymphoid aggregates are positive for 
 REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID , with scattered admixed  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID + T cells.  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  highlights dendritic meshworks 
within lymphoid aggregates. The lymphoid aggregates stain positively for 
bcl-2, and are negative for bcl-6. Lymphoid cells are negative for cyclin  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID . 
 REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  highlights the vasculature; intravascular lymphoid cells are 
inconspicuous. IgD dimly stains some B cells. In-situ hybridization for kappa 
and lambda immunoglobulin light chains shows a few scattered lambda+ plasma 
cells and many scattered kappa+ plasma cells, consistent with a population of 
monotypic kappa+ plasma cells in a small polytypic background. 
 
The findings are consistent with a low-grade B-cell lymphoma with plasmacytic 
differentiation. While the findings are not completely specific, they are most 
consistent with marrow involvement by splenic marginal zone lymphoma.

TEST INFORMATION: 
This assay utilizes a multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology 
called Anchored Multiplex PCR (AMP) for single nucleotide variant (SNV) and 
insertion/deletion (indel) detection in genomic DNA using next generation 
sequencing (NGS). Briefly, genomic DNA was isolated from a formalin-fixed 
paraffin embedded tumor specimen (after histological review for tumor 
enrichment), blood, bone marrow aspirates, or pancreatic cyst fluid. The 
genomic DNA was sheared with the Covaris  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  instrument, followed by 
end-repair, adenylation, and ligation with an adapter. A sequencing library 
targeting hotspots and exons in 39 genes was generated using two hemi-nested PCR 
reactions. Illumina MiSeq 2 x 151 base paired-end sequencing results were 
aligned to the hg19 human genome reference using BWA-MEM [1]. MuTect [2] and a 
laboratory-developed insertion/deletion analysis algorithm were used for SNV and 
indel variant detection, respectively. This assay has been validated to detect 
SNV and indel variants at 5% allelic frequency or higher in target regions with 
sufficient read coverage. Variants are reported with Human Genome Variation 
Society (HGVS) protein and DNA nomenclature, followed by the referenced Ensembl 
transcript ID.

TEST INFORMATION: 
This assay utilizes a multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology

insertion/deletion (indel) detection in genomic DNA using next generation 
sequencing (NGS). Briefly, genomic DNA was isolated from a formalin-fixed 
paraffin embedded tumor specimen (after histological review for tumor 
enrichment), blood, bone marrow aspirates, or pancreatic cyst fluid. The 
genomic DNA was sheared with the Covaris  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  instrument, followed by 
end-repair, adenylation, and ligation with an adapter. A sequencing library 
targeting hotspots and exons in 39 genes was generated using two hemi-nested PCR 
reactions. Illumina MiSeq 2 x 151 base paired-end sequencing results were 
aligned to the hg19 human genome reference using BWA-MEM [1]. MuTect [2] and a 
laboratory-developed insertion/deletion analysis algorithm were used for SNV and 
indel variant detection, respectively. This assay has been validated to detect 
SNV and indel variants at 5% allelic frequency or higher in target regions with 
sufficient read coverage. Variants are reported with Human Genome Variation 
Society (HGVS) protein and DNA nomenclature, followed by the referenced Ensembl 
transcript ID.

TEST INFORMATION: 
Aberrations involving the fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 ( REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID ) gene have 
been noted in tumors of multiple types, including certain lung, breast, ovarian, 
skeletal muscle, melanocytic and hematopoietic neoplasms. [1] Amplification of 
the  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  gene was recently identified as a significant and common finding (22% 
by FISH) in a cohort of squamous cell carcinomas of the lung. [2] 
 
The assay performed on this patient uses fluorescence in situ hybridization 
(FISH) on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor specimens to analyze  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  gene 
amplification status. Briefly, 5-micron sections of formalin-fixed 
paraffin-embedded tumor material were prepared and an H&E section reviewed to 
select regions for hybridization that contain a majority of tumor cells. A

insertion/deletion (indel) detection in genomic DNA using next generation 
sequencing (NGS). Briefly, genomic DNA was isolated from a formalin-fixed

transcript ID.
